[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Network Policies and Microsegmentation in Kubernetes"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, Kubernetes networking is flat: all pods can communicate with all other pods across the cluster. While convenient, this lack of isolation poses severe security risks. If a single pod is compromised, an attacker gains lateral movement across the entire cluster. Kubernetes Network Policies provide a native mechanism to implement microsegmentation, restricting traffic at the IP socket level (OSI Layer 3 and 4)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Prerequisites and CNI Requirements"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before creating Network Policies, ensure your Kubernetes cluster uses a Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin that supports network policy enforcement. Popular choices include Calico, Cilium, Antrea, and AWS VPC CNI. Standard kubenet or basic bridge plugins will accept policy API objects but silently ignore them."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Default Deny All Traffic Strategy"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"A robust microsegmentation strategy starts with a 'Default Deny' posture. This ensures that no pod can send or receive traffic unless explicitly permitted by a rule. Create a namespace-scoped resource to block all ingress and egress traffic."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Allowing Specific Ingress Traffic"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once a default deny policy is active, you must selectively open ports and paths. For example, to allow frontend pods to communicate with backend pods on port 5432 (PostgreSQL), use a targeted Network Policy."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Components of Network Policies"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"podSelector: Determines which pods the policy applies to within the specified namespace. An empty selector ({}) matches all pods."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"policyTypes: Defines whether the policy affects Ingress, Egress, or both."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"namespaceSelector: Allows filtering traffic sources or destinations based on labels attached to entire namespaces."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ports: Restricts traffic to specific protocols and port numbers."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Validation and Troubleshooting"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"To verify that your microsegmentation rules are working properly, you can execute a temporary debugging pod inside the namespace and test connectivity using tools like nc or curl."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"kubectl run tmp-shell --rm -i --tty --image=nicolaka/netshoot --namespace=production -- bash"}]
